subtitle: Map, test, and validate the logic of how your business creates, delivers, and captures value — using proven canvas frameworks.

modules.skill: Map the nine building blocks of any business model and identify how they connect

lessons.title: What Is a Business Model?
lessons.subtitle: It's not a business plan. It's the logic of how you create, deliver, and capture value — and it fits on one page.

cards.headline: The 40-Page Document Nobody Reads
cards.body: Most entrepreneurs spend months writing a business plan. It's a 40-page document that rarely survives first contact with customers. A business model is different — it's the underlying logic of how your business works: who you serve, what you offer, and how money flows. Osterwalder defines it as "the rationale of how an organisation creates, delivers, and captures value." You can sketch one in 20 minutes.

cards.headline: Why Models Beat Plans
cards.body: Plans assume you know the answers. Models assume you have hypotheses to test. A model is visual, shareable, and easy to update. When reality changes (and it will), you pivot the model — not rewrite 40 pages.
bullets: A model can be sketched in 20 minutes, shared in 5
It forces clarity through constraints — one page only
It's designed to be tested and updated, not preserved
Ash Maurya: "Your business model IS your product"

cards.headline: The Three Layers of Value
cards.body: Every sustainable business model answers three questions:
bullets: Value Creation — what problem do you solve and for whom?
Value Delivery — how does the solution reach the customer?
Value Capture — how do you get paid?
cards.statLabel: layers that must all work — if any breaks, the model fails

cards.headline: The Canvas Mindset
cards.body: Instead of writing in isolation for months, you sketch your model on a canvas — a visual chart with building blocks. You share it with your team in minutes. You take it to potential customers and come back with evidence. You update it weekly. This "canvas mindset" treats your business model as a living experiment, not a fixed document.

cards.headline: Your Day 1 Action
cards.body: Grab a blank sheet. Write your business idea in one sentence. Then answer: Who benefits? What do they get? How would you earn revenue? Don't worry about getting it right — this is your first draft, and it will evolve dramatically. The goal today is simply to externalise what's in your head so you can examine and test it.

quiz.question: According to Osterwalder, a business model describes:
options: The rationale of how an organisation creates, delivers, and captures value
A detailed 5-year financial projection
The legal structure of a company
A marketing strategy document
quiz.explanation: A business model is "the rationale of how an organisation creates, delivers, and captures value" — not a financial plan or legal structure.

quiz.question: What is the key advantage of a business model over a business plan?
options: It's longer and more detailed
It assumes you know all the answers
It's visual, testable, and easy to update when reality changes
It satisfies bank requirements for loans
quiz.explanation: Models are designed to be tested and updated quickly, unlike plans that assume certainty and take months to rewrite.

quiz.question: Which is NOT one of the three layers of value in a business model?
options: Value Creation
Value Delivery
Value Regulation
Value Capture
quiz.explanation: The three layers are Value Creation (solve a problem), Value Delivery (reach the customer), and Value Capture (get paid). "Regulation" isn't one of the layers.

lessons.title: The Nine Building Blocks
lessons.subtitle: Meet the Business Model Canvas — nine interconnected blocks that describe any business, from a food truck to a Fortune 500.

cards.headline: One Page That Replaces a Business Plan
cards.body: Created by Alexander Osterwalder, the Business Model Canvas is a strategic tool with nine blocks: Customer Segments, Value Propositions, Channels, Customer Relationships, Revenue Streams, Key Resources, Key Activities, Key Partnerships, and Cost Structure. It forces you to think about your business holistically — not just the product, but the entire system.
cards.statLabel: interconnected blocks that describe any business model

cards.headline: Right Side = Value & Customers
cards.body: The right side of the canvas focuses on value creation and delivery — the "desirability" side:
bullets: Customer Segments — who you serve
Value Propositions — what you offer them
Channels — how you reach them
Customer Relationships — how you interact
Revenue Streams — how you earn from them

cards.headline: Left Side = Infrastructure & Cost
cards.body: The left side focuses on how you deliver — the "feasibility" and "viability" side:
bullets: Key Resources — what you need (assets, IP, people)
Key Activities — what you do (production, problem-solving)
Key Partnerships — who helps you
Cost Structure — what it all costs

cards.headline: How the Blocks Connect
cards.body: The canvas isn't nine independent boxes — it's a system. Your Value Proposition must solve a real problem for your Customer Segment. Your Channels must reach those specific customers. Your Key Activities must deliver that specific value. Your Revenue Streams must exceed your Cost Structure. Change one block and the ripple hits others.

cards.headline: Canvas in Practice: Spotify
cards.body: Customer Segments: music listeners (free & premium). Value Proposition: instant access to millions of songs, personalised discovery. Channels: app stores, web, social sharing. Revenue: subscriptions + ads. Key Resources: licensing deals, recommendation algorithm. Key Partners: record labels, artists. One page reveals the whole business logic at a glance.

quiz.question: How many building blocks does the Business Model Canvas contain?
quiz.explanation: The BMC has exactly nine building blocks that together describe the logic of how a business creates, delivers, and captures value.

quiz.question: The right side of the canvas primarily focuses on:
options: Cost management and efficiency
Value creation and customer desirability
Legal compliance and regulation
Team structure and hiring
quiz.explanation: The right side covers Customer Segments, Value Props, Channels, Relationships, and Revenue — all about desirability and reaching customers.

quiz.question: Why is the canvas described as a "system" rather than independent boxes?
options: Because it must be filled in a specific order
Because changes in one block create ripple effects across others
Because each box requires a separate team
Because it was designed by a systems engineer
quiz.explanation: The blocks are interconnected — changing your Customer Segment affects your Channels, Value Prop, Revenue, and more. It's a holistic system.

lessons.title: Value Propositions That Convert
lessons.subtitle: Your value proposition is the reason customers choose you. Learn to articulate it clearly using the Value Proposition Canvas.

cards.headline: Why Should They Choose You?
cards.body: A value proposition is the bundle of products and services that creates value for a specific customer segment. It answers: "Why should I buy from you instead of your competitor (or instead of doing nothing)?" Great value propositions solve a real pain, deliver a measurable gain, or fulfil a critical job the customer needs done.

cards.headline: The Value Proposition Canvas
cards.body: Osterwalder's Value Proposition Canvas zooms into the fit between what you offer and what customers need:
bullets: Customer Profile: Jobs (what they accomplish), Pains (frustrations), Gains (desired outcomes)
Value Map: Products/Services, Pain Relievers, Gain Creators
Fit happens when your relievers and creators match real pains and gains

cards.headline: Pain Relievers vs Gain Creators
cards.body: Pain Relievers eliminate or reduce specific customer frustrations — saving time, reducing risk, removing anxiety. Gain Creators produce outcomes customers desire — better status, convenience, cost savings. The strongest value propositions do both, but usually lead with pain relief because people are more motivated to eliminate pain than pursue gain (loss aversion).

cards.headline: The "Fit" Spectrum
cards.body: Three levels of fit that every startup must achieve in order:
bullets: Problem-Solution Fit — your proposition addresses real jobs, pains, and gains (on paper)
Product-Market Fit — evidence shows customers want it (they pay, use, recommend)
Business Model Fit — the proposition is embedded in a scalable, profitable model
cards.statLabel: of startups die between Problem-Solution Fit and Product-Market Fit

cards.headline: Craft Your Statement
cards.body: Use this template: "We help [customer segment] who want to [job/gain] by [how you relieve pain/create gain], unlike [alternative] who [limitation]." Example: "We help busy parents who want healthy family meals by delivering pre-portioned recipe kits in 30 minutes, unlike meal planning apps that still require grocery shopping." Specific beats clever.

quiz.question: The Value Proposition Canvas maps the fit between:
options: Competitors and your product features
What you offer and what customers actually need
Revenue streams and cost structure
Marketing channels and customer acquisition
quiz.explanation: The VPC zooms into the relationship between your value map (what you offer) and the customer profile (their jobs, pains, gains).

quiz.question: Why do strong value propositions usually lead with pain relief?
options: Because pain relievers are cheaper to build
Because people are more motivated to eliminate pain than pursue gains
Because gains are impossible to measure
Because investors prefer pain-focused products
quiz.explanation: Loss aversion means people are psychologically more motivated to avoid/eliminate pain than to pursue new gains — pain relief gets faster adoption.

quiz.question: What does "Product-Market Fit" mean in the fit spectrum?
options: Your product has no bugs and works perfectly
Evidence shows customers genuinely want your proposition — they pay, use, or recommend it
You have written a business plan that VCs approve
Your product is listed on a marketplace
quiz.explanation: Product-Market Fit means real evidence (payments, usage, referrals) shows customers want what you're offering — not just that it sounds good on paper.

lessons.title: Customer Segments & Channels
lessons.subtitle: Define exactly who you serve and how you'll reach them. The wrong channel for the right customer is as bad as no channel at all.

cards.headline: The Right Customer, Wrong Channel Problem
cards.body: A customer segment is a group of people with similar needs, behaviours, or attributes. You can segment by: demographics (age, income), behaviour (usage patterns), needs (jobs to be done), or value (willingness to pay). The key question: do they have meaningfully different needs that require a distinct Value Proposition? If yes, they're separate segments.

cards.headline: Multi-Sided Markets
cards.body: Some business models serve two or more interdependent customer segments:
bullets: YouTube serves viewers (free content) and advertisers (paid placement)
Uber serves riders and drivers
Each side has different jobs, pains, gains — and different value propositions
You need critical mass on both sides (the "chicken and egg" challenge)

cards.headline: Channel Phases
cards.body: Channels are how you communicate with and reach customers. Five phases:
bullets: Awareness — how do they learn about you?
Evaluation — how do they assess your proposition?
Purchase — how do they buy?
Delivery — how do you deliver value?
After-sales — how do you provide support?

cards.headline: Channel-Segment Fit
cards.body: Your channel must match your segment's habits. Enterprise customers expect sales reps and demos. Gen Z expects social media and self-serve. Luxury buyers want high-touch experiences. Mapping the wrong channel to the right segment creates friction that kills conversion. Ask: "Where does my customer already spend time?"

cards.headline: Build Your Channel Stack
cards.body: Most businesses need multiple channels working together: content marketing for awareness → free tool for evaluation → website for purchase → email for delivery → community for after-sales. Start with ONE channel that works, then layer others. Spreading across five channels before validating one is a common startup mistake.

quiz.question: What defines a separate customer segment?
options: They live in different countries
They have meaningfully different needs requiring a distinct value proposition
They use different social media platforms
They have different hair colours
quiz.explanation: A distinct segment exists when the group has different enough needs that you need a meaningfully different value proposition to serve them.

quiz.question: Which is the correct order of channel phases?
options: Purchase → Awareness → Delivery → Evaluation → After-sales
Awareness → Evaluation → Purchase → Delivery → After-sales
Delivery → Purchase → Awareness → After-sales → Evaluation
Evaluation → Awareness → Purchase → After-sales → Delivery
quiz.explanation: The five channel phases follow the customer journey: Awareness → Evaluation → Purchase → Delivery → After-sales support.

quiz.question: What is the "chicken and egg" challenge in multi-sided markets?
options: Deciding which product to build first
Needing critical mass on both sides for the model to work
Choosing between different pricing strategies
Finding the right co-founder
quiz.explanation: Multi-sided platforms like Uber need both riders and drivers — but neither side joins without the other already being there.

lessons.title: Revenue & Cost Structure
lessons.subtitle: How money flows in — and out. Design revenue streams that align with customer value and a cost structure that supports your margins.

cards.headline: Seven Ways to Make Money
cards.body: Seven common revenue models: (1) Asset sale — sell a physical/digital product. (2) Usage fee — pay per use (AWS, Uber). (3) Subscription — recurring access (Netflix, SaaS). (4) Licensing — pay for permission to use IP. (5) Brokerage — fee for connecting parties. (6) Advertising — pay for attention. (7) Freemium — free base, paid upgrades. Most businesses combine two or more.
cards.statLabel: revenue model types — most businesses combine 2 or more

cards.headline: Pricing Mechanisms
cards.body: How you set prices matters as much as what you charge:
bullets: Fixed pricing: list prices, volume-dependent, segment-dependent
Dynamic pricing: negotiation, yield management (airlines), auctions, real-time market
Value-based: charge for what matters to them, not what's expensive for you to build

cards.headline: Cost Structure Drivers
cards.body: Two archetypes: Cost-Driven (minimise costs everywhere — low-cost airlines, fast fashion) vs Value-Driven (focus on premium value creation — luxury brands, bespoke services). Key cost categories: fixed costs (rent, salaries), variable costs (materials, commissions), and economies of scale/scope.

cards.headline: Unit Economics
cards.body: Before you scale, you need healthy unit economics:
bullets: Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC) — what you spend to get one customer
Lifetime Value (LTV) — total revenue from that customer over time
LTV:CAC ratio should be at least 3:1 for sustainability
If you spend £100 acquiring a customer who generates £50, growing faster = losing money faster
cards.statLabel: minimum healthy LTV:CAC ratio for sustainable growth

cards.headline: Revenue-Cost Alignment Exercise
cards.body: Map your revenue streams to the value propositions they support. Then map your cost structure to the key activities and resources that deliver those propositions. Ask: "Does every major cost directly enable a value proposition that generates revenue?" If costs don't connect to value creation, they're waste.

quiz.question: What is the minimum healthy LTV:CAC ratio for a sustainable business?
quiz.explanation: A 3:1 ratio means you earn at least £3 for every £1 spent acquiring a customer — the widely accepted minimum for sustainable growth.

quiz.question: Which pricing approach aligns best with customer value perception?
options: Charge based on your development costs
Charge for what matters to customers, not what's expensive to build
Always use the lowest possible price
Copy competitor pricing exactly
quiz.explanation: Value-based pricing charges for what the customer perceives as valuable — which may be very different from what cost you the most to create.

quiz.question: What characterises a "cost-driven" business model?
options: It focuses on premium value creation regardless of cost
It minimises costs across all operations
It charges the highest prices in the market
It only uses fixed costs with no variable expenses
quiz.explanation: Cost-driven models (like Ryanair or Primark) focus on minimising costs wherever possible to compete on price.

lessons.title: Resources, Activities & Partners
lessons.subtitle: The engine room of your model. Identify what you truly need to own, what you must do exceptionally well, and who can help.

cards.headline: The Engine Room of Your Business
cards.body: Resources are the assets required to make your business model work. Four types: Physical (factories, stores, vehicles), Intellectual (patents, brand, proprietary data, algorithms), Human (expert teams, creative talent), Financial (cash, credit lines, investor capital). Not everything you own is a "key" resource — only those essential to your value proposition.

cards.headline: Key Activities
cards.body: These are the most important things you must DO to make the model work:
bullets: Platform businesses: maintain and improve the platform
Product businesses: design, build, deliver
Service businesses: solve customer problems
Identify 3–5 activities that, if stopped, your value proposition collapses

cards.headline: Key Partnerships
cards.body: Four partnership motivations:
bullets: Optimisation & economy of scale — share costs
Risk reduction — spread uncertainty
Acquisition of resources/activities — get what you lack
Strategic alliances — align with complementary businesses

cards.headline: Build vs Buy vs Partner
cards.body: For every resource and activity ask: Should I build it myself (full control, high cost, slow)? Buy it from a vendor (less control, medium cost, fast)? Partner with someone (shared value, shared risk)? Rule of thumb: build only what's core to your unfair advantage. Everything else — buy or partner.

cards.headline: Map Your Engine Room
cards.body: List your top 3 value propositions. For each, identify: What resources are essential to deliver it? What activities must you perform excellently? What partners do you need? If something doesn't connect to a value proposition, question whether it belongs. This reveals bloat (unnecessary resources) and gaps (missing capabilities).

quiz.question: What makes a resource "key" rather than just useful?
options: It's the most expensive item in your budget
It's essential to your value proposition and competitive advantage
It was the first thing you purchased
It has the longest contract term
quiz.explanation: A resource is "key" only if it's essential to delivering your value proposition or maintaining your competitive advantage.

quiz.question: The rule of thumb for "build vs buy vs partner" is:
options: Build everything for maximum control
Build only what's core to your unfair advantage; buy or partner the rest
Always partner to reduce costs
Buy everything to move fastest
quiz.explanation: Focus your limited resources on building what makes you uniquely competitive. For everything else, buying or partnering is faster and cheaper.

quiz.question: Which is NOT a motivation for key partnerships?
options: Optimisation and economy of scale
Reducing competition by acquiring them
Risk reduction
Acquisition of resources or activities you lack
quiz.explanation: The four partnership motivations are: optimisation/scale, risk reduction, resource/activity acquisition, and strategic alliances — not acquiring competitors.

lessons.title: Module 1 Checkpoint
lessons.subtitle: Bring it all together. Map your own business model using all nine blocks and identify the three weakest assumptions.

cards.headline: Your Canvas So Far
cards.body: Over the last six days you've explored all nine building blocks. Now it's time to fill in your own canvas — even if it's rough. Start with your Customer Segments and Value Propositions (the heart of the model), then work outward to Channels, Relationships, Revenue Streams, Resources, Activities, Partners, and Costs.

cards.headline: The Coherence Check
cards.body: A good canvas isn't nine independent answers — it's a coherent story. Test: Can you trace a line from each Customer Segment through a Value Proposition, to Channels that reach them, Relationships that retain them, and Revenue that flows from them? On the left, do your Resources and Activities actually deliver that value? If a block is disconnected, something's wrong.

cards.headline: Spotting Your Weakest Assumptions
cards.body: Every block on your canvas is a hypothesis until proven. Rate each 1-5 (1 = pure guess, 5 = proven). Circle anything below 3 — these are your riskiest assumptions that could sink your model. We'll learn to test them in Module 2.
bullets: Rate evidence strength for each block (1=guess, 5=proven)
Focus on blocks rated below 3
These are your highest-priority experiments

cards.headline: Common Canvas Mistakes
cards.body: Watch for these pitfalls:
bullets: Too many customer segments (focus on one to start)
Feature-focused value prop (list benefits, not features)
"The internet" as a channel (be specific — SEO? YouTube? Cold email?)
No clear revenue model ("we'll figure it out later" = we won't)
Confusing strategic activities with operational tasks

cards.headline: Week 1 Complete — What's Next
cards.body: You now have a full Business Model Canvas — your first hypothesis of how your business works. It's probably wrong in several places, and that's perfect. In Module 2, we'll introduce the Lean Canvas (a startup-optimised variant), and learn to systematically test and validate each block through rapid experimentation.

quiz.question: What is the "coherence check" for a Business Model Canvas?
options: Checking that all boxes are filled in
Verifying you can trace a logical line connecting segments through value, channels, and revenue
Counting the total number of items across all blocks
Getting a mentor to approve your canvas
quiz.explanation: Coherence means the blocks connect logically — you can trace how value flows from creation to delivery to capture for each customer segment.

quiz.question: How should you identify your riskiest assumptions?
options: Ask friends which blocks they like least
Rate each block's evidence 1-5 and focus on anything below 3
Choose the blocks that took longest to fill in
Pick the blocks with the fewest words
quiz.explanation: Rating evidence strength (1=guess, 5=proven) systematically identifies which assumptions are most at risk of being wrong.

quiz.question: Which is a common canvas mistake?
options: Starting with just one customer segment
Listing benefits instead of features in the value proposition
Saying "we'll figure out monetisation later" with no revenue model
Testing assumptions before finalising the canvas
quiz.explanation: "We'll figure out monetisation later" is a common and dangerous mistake — revenue models should be hypothesised from day one, even if they evolve.

lessons.title: The Lean Canvas
lessons.subtitle: Ash Maurya adapted the BMC for startups. Meet the Lean Canvas — faster, riskier assumptions front-and-centre, action-oriented.

cards.headline: A Canvas Built for Startups
cards.body: The Lean Canvas replaces four BMC blocks: Key Partners → Problem, Key Activities → Solution, Key Resources → Key Metrics, Customer Relationships → Unfair Advantage. Why? Startups don't yet have partners or resources — they have problems to solve and hypotheses to test. The Lean Canvas prioritises risk and learning speed over operational completeness.

cards.headline: The Nine Lean Canvas Blocks
cards.body: A different nine from the BMC:
bullets: Problem — top 3 problems for your segment
Customer Segments — who has this problem?
Unique Value Proposition — single clear message
Solution — top 3 features that solve the problem
Channels — path to customers
Revenue Streams / Cost Structure — the money side
Key Metrics — numbers that actually matter
Unfair Advantage — what can't be easily copied

cards.headline: Fill Order Matters
cards.body: Ash Maurya's recommended sequence prevents "solution-first" thinking:
bullets: 1. Problem & Customer Segments (understand the pain)
2. UVP (articulate the value)
3. Solution (only AFTER understanding the problem)
4. Channels and Revenue
5. Cost and Metrics
6. Unfair Advantage last (it often emerges over time)

cards.headline: One Canvas Per Segment
cards.body: Critical rule: create one Lean Canvas per customer segment. Different segments have different problems, value propositions, and channels. Mixing them creates confusion and unfocused strategy. If you have two distinct customer types, you have two business models to test — even if they share the same product.

cards.headline: Your 20-Minute Canvas
cards.body: Set a timer. Pick your most promising customer segment. Fill all nine blocks in 20 minutes. Don't overthink — write your best guesses. This isn't a final document; it's a snapshot of your current hypotheses. The value is making assumptions explicit so you can test them. A messy canvas filled in 20 minutes beats a perfect one you never start.

quiz.question: What does the Lean Canvas replace "Key Partners" with?
options: Problem
Solution
Key Metrics
Unfair Advantage
quiz.explanation: The Lean Canvas replaces Key Partners with Problem because early-stage startups need to validate problems first — partnerships come later.

quiz.question: Why should you fill the Problem block before Solution?
options: Alphabetical order is easier to remember
It prevents "solution-first" thinking and ensures you understand the pain
Solutions are always harder to write
Investors expect problems listed first
quiz.explanation: Starting with Problem ensures you deeply understand the customer pain before jumping to solutions — preventing the trap of building something nobody needs.

quiz.question: Why create one Lean Canvas per customer segment?
options: To use more paper
Different segments have different problems, value props, and channels
To impress investors with more canvases
Because the template only has room for one segment
quiz.explanation: Each segment has distinct pains and needs — mixing them creates unfocused strategy. Separate canvases keep each model clear and testable.

lessons.title: Problem-Solution Fit
lessons.subtitle: Before building anything, verify that real people have the problem you think they have — and that your proposed solution addresses it.

cards.headline: The First Milestone
cards.body: Problem-Solution Fit means you have evidence that: (1) A specific customer segment exists, (2) They have a problem worth solving, (3) Your proposed solution addresses that problem in a way they value. It's the first milestone in the Lean Startup journey — achieved BEFORE you build a product. Most founders skip this and jump straight to building.

cards.headline: The Problem Interview
cards.body: Ash Maurya's Problem Interview has three parts:
bullets: "Tell me about how you [context]..."
"What's the hardest part about [problem area]?"
"How do you deal with it today?"
NEVER mention your solution — test whether the problem exists first
Five conversations can reveal powerful patterns

cards.headline: Signals of a Real Problem
cards.body: Strong vs weak signals to watch for:
bullets: STRONG: Already spending money/time to solve it
STRONG: Describe the pain with emotion
STRONG: Tried multiple workarounds
WEAK: "Yeah, that's kind of annoying"
WEAK: Can't describe current workarounds
Polite interest ≠ real demand

cards.headline: The Solution Interview
cards.body: Once you've validated the problem, demo your PROPOSED solution (a mockup, prototype, or verbal description). Ask: "Does this solve your problem? What's missing? Would you pay for this?" Watch for body language and genuine enthusiasm. The goal: confirm your solution concept fits their problem before investing in development.

cards.headline: Problem-Solution Fit Checklist
cards.body: Check these five boxes before proceeding:
bullets: ✓ I can describe the problem in the customer's own words
✓ At least 5 of 10 interviews confirmed the problem is real
✓ I understand current alternatives and why they fail
✓ My solution addresses the specific pain they described
✓ At least 3 of 5 showed genuine enthusiasm for the concept

quiz.question: During a Problem Interview, when should you mention your solution?
options: At the beginning to set context
In the middle to test reactions
Never — the Problem Interview only validates the problem exists
Only if they ask about it
quiz.explanation: Problem Interviews test whether the problem exists and matters — introducing your solution biases responses. Solutions come in the separate Solution Interview.

quiz.question: Which is a STRONG signal of a real problem?
options: "Yeah, that's kind of annoying"
"Sounds interesting, maybe"
They're already spending money/time trying to solve it
"I never really thought about it"
quiz.explanation: Active spending of time/money on workarounds is strong evidence the problem is real and painful enough that people will pay for a better solution.

quiz.question: Problem-Solution Fit should be achieved:
options: After launching and getting 1000 users
Before building a product — through interviews and concept testing
Only after raising investment
Once revenue exceeds costs
quiz.explanation: Problem-Solution Fit is the FIRST milestone — validated through interviews before investing in building anything.

lessons.title: Unfair Advantage
lessons.subtitle: The hardest box on the Lean Canvas. What do you have that can't be easily copied or bought? Most founders leave it blank — here's how to fill it.

cards.headline: What Can't Be Copied?
cards.body: An unfair advantage is something that cannot be easily copied or bought by competitors. Jason Cohen's list: insider information, personal authority/brand, dream team, existing community, proprietary technology (10x better, not just different), network effects, organic SEO/content moat, and existing customer base. "Working harder" is NOT an unfair advantage.

cards.headline: Why Most Startups Don't Have One (Yet)
cards.body: It's okay to leave this box blank initially. Most unfair advantages are BUILT over time, not inherited. Your first-mover advantage disappears when someone with more resources copies you. But: every customer you serve, every data point you collect, every community member you nurture is building your moat. Be intentional about which advantage you're building toward.

cards.headline: Network Effects — The Strongest Moat
cards.body: Each new user makes the product more valuable for all users:
bullets: LinkedIn: more professionals → more useful for recruiting
Airbnb: more listings → more travellers → more listings
WhatsApp: everyone you know is there → massive switching costs
Once kicked in, competitors face a cold-start problem

cards.headline: Data Moats
cards.body: Every interaction generates data. If you use that data to improve your product (better recommendations, faster results, more personalisation), you create a flywheel: more users → more data → better product → more users. Google Search, Spotify's Discover Weekly, Netflix recommendations — all data moats competitors can't replicate without the same user base.

cards.headline: Building Your Moat Intentionally
cards.body: Ask: "In 18 months, what will I have that a well-funded competitor starting today won't?" Possible answers: deep customer relationships, proprietary dataset, strong brand in niche, loyal community, regulatory approval, exclusive partnerships. Pick one and invest disproportionately. A moat you're actively building beats no moat at all.

quiz.question: Which of these is NOT a valid unfair advantage?
options: Network effects
Working harder than competitors
Proprietary data moat
Existing loyal community
quiz.explanation: "Working harder" can be matched by anyone — it's not defensible. True unfair advantages are structural and can't be easily copied or bought.

quiz.question: What makes network effects the most powerful unfair advantage?
options: They're the cheapest to build
Each new user makes the product more valuable for all users, creating massive switching costs
They require no technology
They work without any users
quiz.explanation: Network effects create a self-reinforcing loop — more users = more value — making it incredibly hard for competitors to lure users away.

quiz.question: It's okay to leave the Unfair Advantage box blank because:
options: It's not an important part of the canvas
Investors don't care about moats
Most unfair advantages are built over time — but be intentional about which one
No business actually has an unfair advantage
quiz.explanation: Moats are built through sustained effort — but leaving it blank forever is dangerous. Be intentional about which advantage you're accumulating.

lessons.title: Metrics That Matter
lessons.subtitle: Not all numbers are created equal. Learn to distinguish vanity metrics from actionable ones and pick the ONE metric that matters most right now.

cards.headline: The Vanity Metric Trap
cards.body: Vanity metrics make you feel good but don't inform decisions: total sign-ups, page views, social followers. Actionable metrics change your behaviour: activation rate, retention at day 7, revenue per user, referral rate. The test: "If this number changed, would we do something differently?" If not, it's vanity.

cards.headline: The One Metric That Matters (OMTM)
cards.body: At any stage, one metric matters more than all others:
bullets: Pre-launch: number of problem interviews completed
Early traction: activation rate (% who experience core value)
Growing: retention (do they come back?)
Scaling: referral rate or LTV:CAC
Optimising everything at once optimises nothing — pick ONE

cards.headline: Pirate Metrics: AARRR
cards.body: Dave McClure's startup metrics framework:
bullets: Acquisition — how do users find you?
Activation — do they have a good first experience?
Retention — do they come back?
Revenue — do they pay?
Referral — do they tell others?
cards.statLabel: funnel stages — your OMTM is the one with the biggest drop-off

cards.headline: Leading vs Lagging Indicators
cards.body: Lagging indicators tell you what happened (revenue this month, churn rate). Leading indicators predict what will happen (trial-to-paid conversion today predicts next month's revenue). Focus on leading indicators because you can still influence them. If your leading indicators are healthy, lagging indicators will follow.

cards.headline: Set Your Key Metrics
cards.body: For your Lean Canvas "Key Metrics" box, list 3–5 metrics that tell you if your model is working. Be specific: not "growth" but "weekly active users increasing 5% week-over-week." Not "engagement" but "average 3 sessions per week per user." Measurable, time-bound, and tied to a threshold.

quiz.question: What makes a metric "vanity"?
options: It's a small number
It makes you feel good but doesn't inform decisions
It's related to social media
It decreases over time
quiz.explanation: Vanity metrics look good on a dashboard but don't change your behaviour or decisions. If the number changed, would you actually do something different?

quiz.question: What does AARRR stand for in Pirate Metrics?
options: Awareness, Action, Retention, Revenue, Referral
Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Revenue, Referral
Acquisition, Activation, Reach, Revenue, Repeat
Advertising, Activation, Retention, Revenue, Reach
quiz.explanation: AARRR = Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Revenue, Referral — Dave McClure's framework for tracking startup growth.

quiz.question: Why focus on leading indicators over lagging ones?
options: Leading indicators are always bigger numbers
You can still influence them — they predict future outcomes you can change
Lagging indicators are always negative
Leading indicators are easier to measure
quiz.explanation: Leading indicators show what's happening NOW and predict the future — giving you time to course-correct before lagging results lock in.

lessons.title: Experiment Design
lessons.subtitle: Turn assumptions into testable hypotheses and design cheap, fast experiments that produce actionable evidence.

cards.headline: From Guess to Hypothesis
cards.body: Every experiment starts with a clear hypothesis: "We believe [specific assumption]. We will test this by [experiment]. We'll know we're right if [measurable outcome] within [timeframe]." Example: "We believe busy parents will pay £8/week for meal kit delivery. We'll test with a landing page and pre-order button. Success = 50+ pre-orders in 2 weeks."

cards.headline: The Experiment Stack
cards.body: From cheapest to most expensive — always start at the top:
bullets: 1. Desk research — Google, forums, existing data (free)
2. Interviews — talk to 5-10 potential customers (time only)
3. Landing page test — measure sign-up intent (£50-100)
4. Concierge MVP — deliver the value manually to a few
5. Wizard of Oz — automated front-end, manual back-end
6. Single-feature MVP — one thing, built properly

cards.headline: Success Criteria (Before You Start)
cards.body: Define what "pass" and "fail" look like BEFORE running the experiment. Otherwise you'll rationalise any result as positive. Be specific: "5% conversion rate on landing page = proceed. Below 2% = pivot. Between 2-5% = iterate messaging." Write it down. Share it. Hold yourself accountable.

cards.headline: Time-Boxing Experiments
cards.body: Every experiment needs a deadline:
bullets: Interviews: 1 week for 10 conversations
Landing page: 2 weeks of traffic
Concierge: 2-4 weeks with 5-10 customers
If you haven't hit criteria by the deadline, the experiment has given its answer

cards.headline: Document Everything
cards.body: For each experiment record: (1) What we believed. (2) What we did. (3) What we observed. (4) What we learned. (5) What we'll do next. This experiment log prevents re-testing disproved hypotheses and shows your rigour. Learning velocity is your startup's most important meta-metric.

quiz.question: Why must you define success criteria BEFORE running an experiment?
options: To impress investors with preparation
To prevent rationalising any result as positive after the fact
Because experiments without criteria run faster
To reduce the cost of the experiment
quiz.explanation: Pre-set criteria prevent confirmation bias — without them, you'll unconsciously interpret ambiguous results as validating your idea.

quiz.question: What is the correct order from cheapest to most expensive experiment?
options: MVP → Landing page → Interviews → Desk research
Desk research → Interviews → Landing page → Concierge → MVP
Interviews → Desk research → MVP → Landing page
Landing page → Interviews → Concierge → Desk research
quiz.explanation: Always start cheap: desk research costs nothing, interviews need only time, landing pages are minimal, before investing in concierge or MVP builds.

quiz.question: What should you do if an experiment hasn't hit criteria by its deadline?
options: Extend the deadline until you get the results you want
Accept the experiment has given its answer — the hypothesis likely failed
Ignore the deadline — deadlines don't apply to startups
Run the same experiment with different people
quiz.explanation: The deadline IS the answer. If you haven't hit threshold by then, the evidence doesn't support your hypothesis.

lessons.title: Pivot or Persevere
lessons.subtitle: The hardest decision in entrepreneurship. Learn the structured framework for knowing when to change direction — and when to double down.

cards.headline: Instagram Started as a Check-In App
cards.body: Eric Ries defines a pivot as "a structured course correction designed to test a new fundamental hypothesis." It's not failure — it's learning. Instagram pivoted from Burbn (a check-in app) to photo-sharing. Slack pivoted from a game to team communication. YouTube started as a video dating site. A pivot keeps one foot planted (what you've learned) while changing direction.

cards.headline: Types of Pivots
cards.body: Ten pivot types to consider:
bullets: Zoom-in — one feature becomes the whole product (Instagram)
Zoom-out — product becomes one feature of a bigger product
Customer segment — same product, different customers
Customer need — same customer, different problem
Channel — different distribution path
Revenue model — different monetisation

cards.headline: The Pivot Decision Framework
cards.body: Ask these four questions:
bullets: 1. Are we making measurable progress toward our success criteria?
2. Is our engine of growth improving week over week?
3. Have we exhausted our current hypothesis space?
4. Do we have a better hypothesis to test?
If answers are No, No, Yes, Yes — it's time to pivot

cards.headline: The "Pivot Meeting"
cards.body: Schedule regular pivot-or-persevere meetings (monthly or after each experiment cycle). Present: Current metrics vs success criteria. What you've learned. What you'd change. This prevents both "zombie startups" (persevering without progress) and "shiny object syndrome" (pivoting too often). Make the decision deliberately, not emotionally.

cards.headline: Avoid These Perseverance Traps
cards.body: Three traps that prevent necessary pivots:
bullets: Sunk cost fallacy — "We've invested too much to change"
Vanity metrics — "But our downloads are growing!"
Optimism bias — "Just one more feature/month/hire"
Counter: "If starting fresh today, would we choose this path?"

quiz.question: What distinguishes a pivot from simply giving up?
options: Pivots happen faster
A pivot keeps one foot planted in learning while changing direction to test a new hypothesis
Giving up involves changing the product name
There is no difference
quiz.explanation: A pivot builds on what you've learned — keeping validated insights while changing the unvalidated elements. It's structured learning, not abandonment.

quiz.question: Instagram's move from Burbn to photo-sharing is an example of:
options: Customer segment pivot
Zoom-in pivot — one feature became the whole product
Revenue model pivot
Technology pivot
quiz.explanation: Instagram "zoomed in" on Burbn's most popular feature — photo sharing — and made it the entire product.

quiz.question: Which is a "perseverance trap" that prevents necessary pivots?
options: Regular pivot-or-persevere meetings
Tracking actionable metrics
Sunk cost fallacy — "We've invested too much to change"
Setting hard experiment deadlines
quiz.explanation: Sunk cost fallacy makes you persist with a failing strategy because of past investment — money already spent shouldn't influence future decisions.

lessons.title: Module 2 Checkpoint
lessons.subtitle: Complete your Lean Canvas, design your first experiment, and set clear pivot-or-persevere criteria.

cards.headline: Canvas to Experiment
cards.body: By now you should have a completed Lean Canvas with all nine blocks filled. Review it with fresh eyes: Is the Problem block based on real customer conversations (not assumptions)? Does the UVP clearly state why you're different? Is the Solution the simplest possible version that addresses the problem? Are your Metrics specific and measurable?

cards.headline: Your Riskiest Assumption
cards.body: Look at your canvas. Which single assumption, if wrong, would kill the entire model? Common killers:
bullets: "Customers have this problem" (they might not)
"They'll pay this much" (they might pay less or nothing)
"We can reach them through this channel" (it might not work)
Circle it — this is experiment #1

cards.headline: Design Experiment #1
cards.body: Take your riskiest assumption and apply the framework: Hypothesis ("We believe..."), Test (choose from experiment stack — start cheap), Success criteria (specific numbers), Deadline (1-2 weeks). Write it down right now. If you leave this lesson without a concrete experiment plan, you'll likely never test your assumption.

cards.headline: Set Pivot Criteria Now
cards.body: Before you run the experiment, write down: "If [success criteria] is NOT met by [deadline], we will [specific action]." Options: pivot the customer segment, pivot the solution, pivot the channel, or abandon. Setting criteria while rational prevents emotional decision-making when results arrive.

cards.headline: Module 2 Complete — Your Toolkit
cards.body: You now have:
bullets: ✓ A completed Lean Canvas (snapshot of current hypotheses)
✓ Understanding of Problem-Solution Fit and how to achieve it
✓ Clarity on the unfair advantage you're building
✓ Key metrics that actually matter (not vanity)
✓ An experiment designed and ready to run
✓ Pivot criteria set in advance

quiz.question: What should your first experiment always test?
options: The easiest assumption to prove
The assumption that would kill your entire model if wrong
The most impressive-sounding hypothesis
Whatever your co-founder wants to test
quiz.explanation: Test the riskiest assumption first — if it's wrong, everything else doesn't matter. Most efficient use of limited time and resources.

quiz.question: Why set pivot criteria BEFORE running an experiment?
options: Because you might forget to write them later
To impress your team with preparation
To prevent emotional decision-making when results arrive
Because investors require documented criteria
quiz.explanation: Setting criteria while rational prevents you from moving goalposts or rationalising poor results when emotions are high.

quiz.question: Which indicates your Lean Canvas Problem block needs rework?
options: It has more than three items listed
It was written based on assumptions without customer conversations
The handwriting is messy
It doesn't mention competitors
quiz.explanation: Problems based on assumptions (not evidence) are the #1 reason startups build things nobody wants. Interview first, then fill the canvas.

lessons.title: The Build-Measure-Learn Loop
lessons.subtitle: The engine of the Lean Startup. Learn to cycle through ideas faster than your competition — turning uncertainty into knowledge.

cards.headline: The Engine of Innovation
cards.body: Eric Ries's Build-Measure-Learn loop is the core engine of the Lean Startup. You build the smallest possible thing to test a hypothesis, measure the results against your success criteria, and learn whether to pivot or persevere. Then repeat. The goal isn't to build a perfect product — it's to learn as fast as possible what customers actually want.

cards.headline: Plan in Reverse: Learn → Measure → Build
cards.body: While you execute Build → Measure → Learn, you should PLAN in reverse:
bullets: 1. What do we need to LEARN? (The assumption to validate)
2. How will we MEASURE it? (The metric and threshold)
3. What's the minimum we need to BUILD? (The smallest experiment)
This prevents over-building — you only build what's needed to learn

cards.headline: Speed Is Everything
cards.body: Your competitive advantage as a startup isn't resources — it's learning speed. Every loop teaches you something. The faster you cycle, the more you learn. If you can run one BML loop per week while a competitor does one per month, you'll have 4x the validated learning in the same time. Minimise the time through each loop.
cards.statLabel: learning advantage from weekly cycles vs monthly ones

cards.headline: Common BML Mistakes
cards.body: Traps to avoid in the loop:
bullets: Building too much before measuring (weeks of dev without customer contact)
Measuring the wrong thing (vanity metrics that don't inform decisions)
Not learning explicitly (collecting data but never sitting down to interpret it)
Skipping the "decide" step (measuring but never making pivot/persevere decisions)

cards.headline: Your First Loop
cards.body: Take your experiment from Lesson 12. Frame it as a BML loop: What are you building? (The experiment — keep it minimal.) What are you measuring? (Your success metric + threshold.) What will you learn? (Whether your riskiest assumption holds.) Set a 1-week deadline for one complete loop. Go.

quiz.question: How should you PLAN a Build-Measure-Learn loop?
options: Start with what's easiest to build
In reverse: decide what to Learn, then how to Measure, then what to Build
Start with the most impressive feature
Copy what competitors are building
quiz.explanation: Planning in reverse (Learn → Measure → Build) ensures you only build the minimum needed to get the learning you seek.

quiz.question: What is the startup's primary competitive advantage according to Lean Startup?
options: More funding than competitors
Better technology
Learning speed — cycling through BML loops faster
A larger team
quiz.explanation: Startups can't compete on resources — they compete on speed of learning. Faster BML loops = more validated knowledge per unit of time.

quiz.question: Which is a common Build-Measure-Learn mistake?
options: Running loops too quickly
Building too much before measuring — weeks of dev without customer contact
Talking to customers too often
Setting success criteria in advance
quiz.explanation: Over-building before measuring wastes time and resources — you might spend weeks building something customers don't want.

lessons.title: Minimum Viable Product
lessons.subtitle: The MVP is the smallest thing you can build to start the learning loop. But "minimum" doesn't mean ugly — it means focused.

cards.headline: Minimum ≠ Terrible
cards.body: An MVP is "that version of a new product which allows a team to collect the maximum amount of validated learning about customers with the least effort" (Ries). It's NOT a half-baked, buggy mess. It's the smallest thing that delivers real value to real users AND teaches you whether your model works. Quality matters — but scope doesn't.

cards.headline: MVP Types
cards.body: Different MVPs test different assumptions:
bullets: Landing page MVP — tests demand ("Will people sign up?")
Concierge MVP — deliver value manually to 5-10 customers
Wizard of Oz — looks automated, but you're behind the curtain
Single-feature MVP — one thing done excellently
Crowdfunding MVP — tests willingness to pay before building

cards.headline: What Your MVP Must Have
cards.body: Every MVP needs these three elements: (1) A clear value proposition — users must understand what they get. (2) A core experience — they must actually experience the primary value. (3) A feedback mechanism — you must learn something from their behaviour. If your MVP doesn't teach you something, it's just a prototype.

cards.headline: The "Will They Use It?" vs "Can We Build It?" Trap
cards.body: Most founders focus their MVP on proving they can build the solution (feasibility). But the biggest risk is usually that customers won't use it (desirability). Test desirability first. If nobody wants it, it doesn't matter if you can build it brilliantly. Feasibility MVPs come after you've proven demand.
cards.statLabel: of startup failures are due to lack of demand, not lack of technology

cards.headline: Design Your MVP
cards.body: What's your riskiest assumption? Choose the MVP type that tests it with least effort. Define: what's included (1-3 features max), what's excluded (everything else), who are your first 10 users, and what metric proves success. If you can't describe your MVP in one sentence, it's too complex.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of an MVP?
options: To launch a finished product as quickly as possible
To collect maximum validated learning with least effort
To build the cheapest possible version of your full vision
To satisfy investor requirements for a demo
quiz.explanation: An MVP's purpose is learning — collecting the most validated knowledge about customers with the minimum investment of time and resources.

quiz.question: What's the biggest risk most MVPs should test FIRST?
options: Feasibility — can we build it?
Scalability — can it handle millions of users?
Desirability — will customers actually want and use it?
Profitability — will it make money on day one?
quiz.explanation: 90% of startups fail due to lack of demand. Test desirability (will they use it?) before feasibility (can we build it?).

quiz.question: What three elements must every MVP have?
options: Logo, website, and social media
Clear value proposition, core experience, and feedback mechanism
Investor deck, roadmap, and team page
Three features, a database, and user authentication
quiz.explanation: Users must understand the value (proposition), experience it (core), and their behaviour must teach you something (feedback).

lessons.title: Innovation Accounting
lessons.subtitle: Traditional accounting can't measure progress for startups. Learn the alternative framework that tracks validated learning.

cards.headline: When Revenue = Zero, How Do You Measure Progress?
cards.body: Traditional metrics (revenue, profit) are meaningless for early startups — they're all zero or near-zero. Innovation accounting measures progress differently: Are you learning? Are your key metrics improving? Are you reducing risk? It's a framework for demonstrating that your experiments are generating real progress toward a sustainable business.

cards.headline: The Three Steps of Innovation Accounting
cards.body: Eric Ries's framework:
bullets: 1. Establish the baseline — measure where you are now (current conversion, retention, etc.)
2. Tune the engine — run experiments to move those metrics toward your ideal
3. Pivot or persevere — if metrics aren't improving despite effort, pivot
Each step produces concrete evidence of progress or failure

cards.headline: Cohort Analysis
cards.body: Instead of looking at cumulative totals (vanity), look at cohorts — groups of users who started in the same time period. Compare: Week 1 users vs Week 4 users. Are newer cohorts performing better? Higher activation? Better retention? If yes, your experiments are working. If not, you're optimising the wrong things.

cards.headline: The Engine of Growth
cards.body: Three engines that drive sustainable growth:
bullets: Sticky — high retention, low churn (subscription products)
Viral — users bring other users (referral loops, social products)
Paid — profitable customer acquisition (LTV > CAC)
Pick ONE engine to optimise first — don't split focus across all three

cards.headline: Set Up Your Innovation Dashboard
cards.body: Create a simple dashboard with: (1) Your OMTM and its current value. (2) The target value you need to hit. (3) Which engine of growth you're optimising. (4) This week's experiment and its result. (5) Trend line — is the metric improving week over week? Update weekly. This is your progress evidence.

quiz.question: Why can't traditional accounting measure startup progress?
options: Startups don't have bank accounts
Traditional metrics (revenue, profit) are all zero/near-zero for early startups
Accountants don't understand technology
Traditional accounting is too expensive
quiz.explanation: Early startups have no revenue to measure — innovation accounting tracks validated learning and metric improvements instead.

quiz.question: What is cohort analysis?
options: Comparing total user numbers month over month
Comparing groups of users from the same time period to see if newer cohorts perform better
Analysing your team's performance reviews
Measuring how many investors you've spoken to
quiz.explanation: Cohort analysis compares user groups from different time periods — if newer cohorts have better metrics, your optimisations are working.

quiz.question: Which is NOT one of the three engines of growth?
options: Sticky (high retention)
Viral (users bring users)
Organic (SEO traffic)
Paid (LTV > CAC)
quiz.explanation: Ries's three engines are Sticky, Viral, and Paid. SEO may feed the paid or viral engine, but isn't a standalone engine in this framework.

lessons.title: Product-Market Fit Signals
lessons.subtitle: How do you know when you've found it? Learn the quantitative and qualitative signals that tell you your model is working.

cards.headline: You'll Feel It (If You Know What to Look For)
cards.body: Marc Andreessen: "You can always feel when product-market fit isn't happening... customers aren't getting value, word of mouth isn't spreading. And you can always feel when product-market fit IS happening... customers are buying as fast as you can supply." But feelings aren't reliable — here are the measurable signals.

cards.headline: The Sean Ellis Test
cards.body: Ask your users: "How would you feel if you could no longer use [product]?" If 40%+ say "Very disappointed," you likely have PMF. Below 25% means you have significant work to do. Between 25-40% is promising but not there yet. This single question cuts through noise because it measures genuine dependency, not politeness.

cards.headline: Quantitative PMF Signals
cards.body: Numbers that indicate product-market fit:
bullets: Retention curve flattens (users stop leaving after initial drop)
Organic/word-of-mouth growth > 50% of new users
NPS > 50 (more promoters than detractors)
Users engage more over time, not less
LTV:CAC ratio exceeds 3:1

cards.headline: Qualitative PMF Signals
cards.body: Behaviours and patterns that indicate fit:
bullets: Users complain when the product is down (they depend on it)
They tell others without being asked (organic referrals)
They use it in ways you didn't expect (hacking it for their needs)
They ask for more features in adjacent areas (want to go deeper)
Sales cycles shorten dramatically (less convincing needed)

cards.headline: Measure Your Current PMF Score
cards.body: If you have users, run the Sean Ellis test this week. Send a simple survey: "How would you feel if you could no longer use [product]?" with options: Very disappointed / Somewhat disappointed / Not disappointed / N/A. You need at least 40 responses for statistical significance. If you don't have users yet, define which signal you'll track first.

quiz.question: What percentage saying "Very disappointed" indicates product-market fit?
quiz.explanation: Sean Ellis established 40%+ "Very disappointed" responses as the benchmark for product-market fit.

quiz.question: Which is a quantitative signal of product-market fit?
options: Users say nice things in interviews
Retention curve flattens — users stop leaving after the initial drop
You have a beautiful website design
Investors are interested in your pitch
quiz.explanation: A flattening retention curve means users who stay past the initial period continue to stay — they've found lasting value.

quiz.question: Which qualitative signal suggests you might have PMF?
options: Users politely fill out your surveys
Users complain when the product is down — they depend on it
Users visit your website once
Users follow you on social media
quiz.explanation: When users complain about downtime, they depend on your product — it's become essential to their workflow. That's a strong PMF signal.

lessons.title: Business Model Patterns
lessons.subtitle: Don't reinvent the wheel. Study proven patterns used by the world's most successful companies and adapt them to your context.

cards.headline: Patterns, Not Inventions
cards.body: Most successful business models aren't invented from scratch — they're adaptations of proven patterns applied in new contexts. Osterwalder identified recurring patterns across industries. Understanding these patterns gives you a "menu" of tested approaches. Your innovation is in which pattern you choose and how you apply it to your specific market.

cards.headline: The Freemium Pattern
cards.body: Give the core product away free to a large user base. Convert a small percentage (2-5%) to premium. Examples: Spotify, LinkedIn, Dropbox. Key metrics: free-to-paid conversion rate, viral spread of free tier, feature differentiation between tiers. Works when: marginal cost per free user is near-zero, and value increases enough at premium to justify paying.
cards.statLabel: typical free-to-paid conversion rate in freemium models

cards.headline: The Platform Pattern
cards.body: Connect two or more groups who need each other:
bullets: Marketplace: Airbnb (hosts ↔ guests), Uber (drivers ↔ riders)
Revenue: transaction fees, listing fees, or ads
Challenge: chicken-and-egg — who joins first?
Moat: network effects make switching costly
Strategy: subsidise one side to attract the other

cards.headline: The Razor-and-Blade Pattern
cards.body: Sell the "razor" cheaply (or free), make money on recurring "blades." Examples: Printers (cheap) + ink (expensive). Game consoles (subsidised) + games (high margin). Nespresso machines (affordable) + pods (premium). Works when lock-in is strong and switching costs are high. Risk: competitors can offer compatible "blades" at lower prices.

cards.headline: Pattern-Match Your Model
cards.body: Look at your current business model canvas. Which pattern does it most closely resemble? Could a different pattern serve your customers better? Try sketching your model using two different patterns and compare. Sometimes switching from "sell a product" to "platform connecting buyers and sellers" or "subscription" transforms the entire economics.

quiz.question: What free-to-paid conversion rate is typical for freemium models?
quiz.explanation: 2-5% conversion from free to paid is typical — which means you need a massive free base to build a significant revenue stream.

quiz.question: What creates the "moat" in platform business models?
options: Patent protection
Network effects — more users makes switching costly
Government regulation
Lower prices than competitors
quiz.explanation: Platforms become harder to compete with as they grow — network effects mean more users = more value, creating massive switching costs.

quiz.question: In the razor-and-blade pattern, where is the profit made?
options: On the initial "razor" sale
On recurring "blade" purchases (consumables)
On advertising alongside the product
On reselling the razor after use
quiz.explanation: The razor (printer, console, machine) is sold cheaply to create lock-in; profit comes from recurring blade (ink, games, pods) purchases.

lessons.title: Scaling Your Validated Model
lessons.subtitle: Once you have product-market fit, it's time to pour fuel on the fire. But scale the right things in the right order.

cards.headline: Don't Scale Before You're Ready
cards.body: Premature scaling is the #1 cause of startup death (Startup Genome Report). Scaling before product-market fit is like pouring fuel on a fire that isn't lit — you waste resources and accelerate failure. But once you have real PMF signals, NOT scaling is equally dangerous. Competitors will fill the vacuum. Timing is everything.
cards.statLabel: cause of startup death: premature scaling before product-market fit

cards.headline: The Scaling Readiness Checklist
cards.body: Scale only when:
bullets: ✓ Sean Ellis score > 40% "Very disappointed"
✓ Retention curve has flattened
✓ Unit economics are healthy (LTV:CAC > 3:1)
✓ You have a repeatable acquisition channel
✓ Operational processes can handle 10x volume

cards.headline: What to Scale First
cards.body: Scale in this order: (1) Your engine of growth — whatever's already working (paid, viral, or sticky). (2) Your team — hire for the bottleneck, not broadly. (3) Your infrastructure — only when current systems are breaking. (4) Your product surface — expand features AFTER your core is unshakeable. Most founders scale product first when they should scale distribution first.

cards.headline: Scaling Risks
cards.body: Common dangers during scaling:
bullets: Losing touch with customers (layers between you and users)
Breaking what works (changing the core while scaling)
Hiring too fast (culture dilution, communication overhead)
Over-expanding scope (serving new segments before nailing the first)
Running out of cash (scaling is expensive — revenue must keep up)

cards.headline: Your Scale Plan
cards.body: Even if you're pre-PMF, sketch your scaling plan: What would you scale first if metrics hit your targets tomorrow? What's your engine of growth? What's the first hire you'd make? What's the first system that would break at 10x? Having this plan ready means you won't waste the PMF moment when it arrives.

quiz.question: What is the #1 cause of startup death according to the Startup Genome Report?
options: Running out of funding
Premature scaling before product-market fit
Co-founder disagreements
Lack of technical talent
quiz.explanation: Premature scaling — growing before validating — wastes resources and accelerates failure. It's the most common killer of startups.

quiz.question: What should you typically scale FIRST after achieving PMF?
options: Product features — add as many as possible
Your engine of growth — whatever acquisition channel is already working
Your team — hire across all departments simultaneously
Your office space — move to a bigger location
quiz.explanation: Scale what's already working (your proven growth engine) before expanding product scope or hiring broadly.

quiz.question: Which is a scaling readiness signal?
options: You have a great product idea
Retention curve has flattened and unit economics are healthy
You've raised a large investment round
Your website has a lot of traffic
quiz.explanation: Flat retention (users stay) + healthy unit economics (LTV > 3x CAC) = the model works and scaling won't just amplify losses.

lessons.title: Module 3 Checkpoint
lessons.subtitle: Bring together everything you've learned. You now have a complete toolkit for designing, testing, and scaling a business model.

cards.headline: From Blank Canvas to Validated Model
cards.body: Three weeks ago, you had an idea. Now you have: a Business Model Canvas mapping your full system, a Lean Canvas focused on your riskiest hypotheses, an experiment framework for testing assumptions, metrics that matter, and criteria for knowing when to pivot or scale. That's not a business plan — it's a living learning system.

cards.headline: Your Complete Journey
cards.body: The three-module progression:
bullets: Module 1: Map your model — understand all nine blocks and how they connect
Module 2: Test your model — Lean Canvas, experiments, pivot decisions
Module 3: Iterate to fit — BML loops, MVP, PMF signals, scaling
This is a cycle, not a line — you'll loop back through these stages many times

cards.headline: The Model Is Never "Done"
cards.body: Even after PMF, your business model will evolve. New competitors change your positioning. New technology enables new channels. Customer needs shift. Markets expand. The canvas mindset — sketch, test, iterate — applies forever. The companies that thrive are those that continuously redesign their models before they're forced to.

cards.headline: Your Next Steps
cards.body: Immediate actions to take:
bullets: Complete (or update) your Lean Canvas with everything you've learned
Run your first experiment this week — don't let knowledge sit idle
Schedule a weekly pivot-or-persevere review (even if it's just you)
Pick your One Metric That Matters and track it daily
Share your canvas with one trusted person for feedback

cards.headline: Course Complete — Congratulations! 🎉
cards.body: You've completed "Design Your Business Model." You now have the frameworks used by the world's most successful entrepreneurs. But frameworks without action are just theory. Your challenge: run one complete Build-Measure-Learn loop within the next 7 days. That single loop will teach you more than any course ever could.

quiz.question: Why is business model design described as "a cycle, not a line"?
options: Because it takes exactly 21 days to complete
Because you'll loop back through mapping, testing, and iterating many times as markets change
Because it goes in a circle on the page
Because you need to take the course again
quiz.explanation: Business models constantly evolve — you'll revisit each stage as customers, competitors, and markets change. It's an ongoing process.

quiz.question: What should you do within 7 days of completing this course?
options: Write a 40-page business plan
Run one complete Build-Measure-Learn loop
Quit your job to focus on your startup
Raise investment funding
quiz.explanation: One real BML loop teaches more than theory alone. Taking action immediately turns knowledge into validated learning.

quiz.question: Even after product-market fit, your business model should:
options: Never be changed again
Be locked in and only optimised for efficiency
Continue to evolve as competitors, technology, and markets shift
Be abandoned for a completely new model
quiz.explanation: Models must continuously evolve — companies that stop adapting get disrupted. The canvas mindset applies forever.
